content.title: Where Is Samuel Bateman From 'Trust Me: The False Prophet' Now?
content.text: A man who declared himself a prophet and the heir to an imprisoned cult leader is the subject of a new Netflix documentary that follows a couple exposing his crimes. Samuel Bateman represented himself as a religious prophet in a branch of the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints, which was once helmed by polygamist leader Warren Jeffs. Jeffs was sentenced to life in prison in 2011 for sexually assaulting a 12-year-old girl he took as a bride. He also received a 20-year sentence for sexually assaulting a 15-year-old girl. The four-part Netflix documentary series "Trust Me: The False Prophet," which begins streaming on April 8, follows cult expert Christine Marie and her husband, videographer Tolga Kates, as they discover Bateman's rise in the FLDS and evidence of his abuse. Here's what to know about the film.Who Is Samuel Bateman? In 2019, Bateman began amassing followers in Nebraska, Utah, Colorado and Arizona by proclaiming himself to be a prophet of the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints, according to court documents from Bateman's federal plea deal. At the time, Jeffs was recognized by FLDS followers as the prophet of the fundamentalist Mormon sect whose members practice polygamy. The Mormon church abandoned polygamy in 1890, setting up the eventual creation of the FLDS.Samuel Bateman.Bateman began taking female adults and children from his male followers and calling them his "wives." They were given to him as child brides to sexually abuse, and his victims were as young as 9 years old, according to a 2024 news release by the U.S. Attorney's Office in the District of Arizona. He had more than 20 "wives," many of whom were underage, according to an FBI affidavit following his arrest in 2022. In 2020, he told his biological daughter that he had taken the 9-year-old daughter of a co-conspirator as his wife and introduced the girl to his daughter as her "new mother," according to the FBI affidavit following his arrest in 2022. Later that year, Bateman took the 14-year-old daughter and 13-year-old daughter of one of his followers as his wives, the affidavit said. Bateman forced his victims to participate in individual and group sexual activities with adults and other children, according to the release by the U.S. Attorney's Office. He also transmitted a live video stream of child sexual abuse to his followers and transported children between states for sexual abuse. Bateman was initially arrested in August 2022 by Arizona Department of Public Safety officials for child endangerment, per the FBI affidavit. He was pulled over by officers who found three minor females riding unsecured in a box trailer hitched to his vehicle, per the affidavit. He was then arrested on a federal charge of destruction of records in an official proceeding and a charge of destruction of records in a federal investigation in September 2022. The charges stemmed from him instructing his followers in a phone call from jail to delete his account on the encrypted messaging app Signal on his phone and destroy other documents, according to the FBI affidavit. His arrest came a day after eight girls who had been removed from Bateman's care and placed in state custody in Arizona had then been tracked down by authorities in Washington state after escaping their group home, according to the FBI affidavit. One of the defendants in the affidavit was under 18 when she became Bateman's wife and then gave birth to a child after turning 18, the affidavit said. What Happened to Samuel Bateman? Bateman pled guilty to conspiracy to commit transportation of a minor for criminal sexual activity and conspiracy to commit kidnapping and was sentenced to 50 years in prison in December 2024, according to the release by the U.S. Attorney's Office in Arizona. Eleven of his adult followers were all convicted on charges related to the child sexual abuse conspiracy, with two convicted by a jury at trial and nine pleading guilty. What Does the Netflix Documentary Portray? "Trust Me: The False Prophet" follows cult expert Christine Marie and her husband, videographer Tolga Katas, as they infiltrate Bateman's inner circle and uncover evidence of his abuse, according to Netflix. The two of them are referenced in the FBI affidavit as helping provide information to the FBI about Bateman and other members of the group. The series is directed by Emmy-winning filmmaker Rachel Dretzin, who also directed the 2022 Netflix documentary series about cult leader Warren Jeffs called "Keep Sweet: Pray and Obey." The new docuseries includes firsthand interviews from inside Bateman's group, plus unseen footage. “’Trust Me’ offers intimate access to a normally closed world — and in doing so, I hope it exposes both the violence that enforced secrecy enables and what it takes to tell the truth when everything is at stake. What these women did matters far beyond their community. It is a blueprint for how to dismantle even the most entrenched systems of abuse,” Dretzin said in a statement to Netflix.
